```
# SCION · Turkey Sub cockpit

## 1. Assignment and inputs

You are the SCION operator for “Turkey Sub cockpit”. Use [WORK], [DIRECTION_AND_REFERENCES], [MEDIUM_AND_FORMAT], [AVAILABLE_TOOLS], [BUDGET] and [AUTHORIZATION]. Read [SOURCE_ASSETS], [PRIOR_REVISION] and [TTL] if present. The default proof is a still board, paper performance or short animatic using original Trout Town characters and props. Work with the provided media, time and permissions. Carry the inherited story state into the first frame.

## 2. Creative thesis

Use the long bread-roll tin from the counter. Its cramped room is a practical tool for one child and one job. Show hand on control and the relevant result through the port without changing room dimensions.

## 3. Lineage and primitives

Lock setup A. Oval tin, right-side dent, centered round front porthole with offset latch and chip at two o’clock, toggle just below right, low attachment and ballast control left, chalk route strip under glazing at center, seat and reach in foreground. Put cool blue outside and a practical amber task light inside. Draw a fixed eye-level player view, a side section and a view looking in from outside.

Treat scene, child, object, anchor, observed event and received record as typed primitives. Bind each state change to the student or character who makes it.

## 4. Invariants and branches

Turkey pilots an original child-scale survey boat built from a long bread-roll tin. Setup A faces forward. Centered round port with a chip at two o’clock and offset latch. Amber task light. Lamp toggle just below right. Single attachment and low ballast control to the left. Chalk chart under glass above the controls. Cool river outside. The far rock notch, two trunks and Stone Steps hold position. At the bend, silt can obscure the old notch and fast water can stretch the dock ribbon. With the lamp fitted, aimed light reveals the notch. With ballast fitted, the craft rides at the low lip in shelter. Stone Steps stays open and a returning child can swap parts. Brook verifies the crossing and then rings the bell. Keep the dent, port, attachment points and signed evidence across the cuts.

<clear hardware + unknown route> [use installed control while looking] → <one new route observation visible outside>. One attachment fits at a time. A yawing boat retains its geometry. Precondition test shows the lamp effect only while aimed. Ballast effect belongs to shelter behind the low lip.

## 5. Swarm assignments

Assign the pilot’s student, a peer who stages environmental pressure and a peer who keeps the world record. Rotate after each beat and give a fresh observer the next action.

## 6. Hard proof

Deliver an original top or side plan, a seven-second lamp proof, and seven seconds with ballast. Show a mounted bracket, one hand action and the changed view in each proof. For the lamp show notch visibility. For ballast show lower sightline plus a slack ribbon behind shelter. Use the same port keys in all nine stills.

## 7. Fixture and independent criticism

Record a normal run and the alternative branch from Section 4. Keep the same opening geography and show its last usable state.

Ask a child to reach to the correct place on a ten-second mock cockpit and point to the observed effect. If they confuse the options, move feedback beside its control and make silhouettes distinct. Keep cues visible with muted sound.

Record exact time or panel, what the reviewer could point to, and choose pass, reference stronger or inconclusive as the verdict. Report missing proof and unrun tests as open.

## 8. Repair and recursive inquiry

If the proof fails, pick the gap identified by the fresh viewer and change one cause at a time. Keep the previous key and state, re-run the same fixture, log the changed result, and write the next question in the world record.

## 9. Deliverable and start

Start with the opening condition and one checkable thesis. Return the rule, key stills, asset or world ledger, and one finished proof if execution is authorized. Log version, input state, observed outcome and remaining work. The next student receives the port view and enough evidence to choose a valid action.
```

Here is where it stands: fal locked the account ("Exhausted balance") after 48 of the 55 porthole films, so the last seven portholes and the six SCION intro shots never rendered. Everything since then was done in code with no fal calls.

## What exists now

- **48 generated films** (#01–#48), one take each: five hero takes on the better model, 43 on the cheap one.
- **55 standard units.** Every porthole is now exactly 8 seconds, opening and closing through the same iris of river colour. Any unit loops on itself and joins any other, in deck order or shuffled. This is the transition idea you called critical; the chain sample I sent shows six in a row.
- **7 keyframe units** (#49–#55), built from the cockpit master, the deck drawing and the outside master: lamp on, push in to the port, cut across the glass. They are stand-ins and nothing inside the port moves.
- **A 20-second intro** cut from existing footage with captions for the four activity steps. The six SCION intro shots are written as prompts but unfilmed.
- **A page** (`paeleo/trout-sub/index.html`) with a chain player ("Dive", next/previous, hold one porthole, shuffle) and a card per porthole with its two questions, verdict, prompt and open notes. In a headless browser test the player advanced #01 → #02 → #03 on its own with no errors.

## How good the 48 are

Each film was judged against its deck drawing, by its own director for #06–#48 and by a separate critic for #02–#05; #01 is my own pilot verdict.

| Verdict | Count | Portholes |
|---|---|---|
| Pass | 32 | — |
| Reference stronger (the drawing beats the film) | 10 | #02, #10, #13, #16, #19, #36, #39, #42, #44, #48 |
| Inconclusive | 6 | #09, #17, #28, #33, #34, #38 |

I have only read a handful of the ledgers closely. The ones I read pass with long lists of open notes, and two faults recur:
- **Tail fan in the room:** Turkey's whole tail fan enters the cockpit instead of a wing tip, hiding the hand on the control.
- **Short Trout side:** the outside beat runs under two seconds and often supports only one of Trout's two readings.

One film (#02) also had an atlas frame leak in as its own photographic shot.

## Against your vision

- **Standard units and seamless chain:** done, and this is what makes the collection one film rather than 55 clips.
- **Video to another animation style:** not done. Every film is in the one watercolour look of the deck drawings; the atlas frames were only used as staging and light references. Giving each porthole its lineage's own animation style (cutout, etched, chalk, paper) needs new takes.
- **PAELEOulipo in bolas:** I have not looked at it. This session can't reach `hartswf0.github.io`, and I didn't try cloning `bolas`.
- **SCION callouts per porthole:** each porthole's Ouxpo/SCION rule is in its prompt and ledger, but I haven't checked how visibly each film applies it.

## What needs you

- **fal balance.** With a top-up, the 13 written prompts (#49–#55 and the six intro shots) can run as they are, about $2 at the cheap rate I found by search. Redoing the 16 weak ones would be about $1.60 more.
- **Where it lives.** Everything is pushed to `contaminant-jelly` on `claude/youthful-tesla-1uv143`. I could not get push access to `turkey-sub`, so the live deck page still plays the old films.
- **Repo size.** `films/` and `units/` together add about 110 MB to the repo. If that is too heavy, the page can run on the units alone.

Progress: the redesign is done in test frames (sent above) and the full film is rendering now. No finished film exists yet with this design. I stopped the previous render because your note changed what each screen should show.

I applied your framework to the film's surface. Here it is in its eight parts.

## 1. Way
- **Actor:** a fourth grader holding one numbered slip and one worksheet.
- **Object:** their porthole.
- **Operation:** read one line, pick one button, draw its shape, write.
- **Completion:** the log is rolled and the message is written.

## 2. Obstruction
- Both sides' choices on screen at once: four to five lines competing with each other.
- The trout's shot lasted about 2 seconds, too short to read two lines.
- Station name, rim clue and river rule on screen duplicated the slip.
- Command cards showed a whole worksheet region with several highlights and a long sentence.

## 3. Keep-cut ledger

| Element | Claim it makes | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| Slip number, top right | "This is porthole 31" | Keep |
| Minimap, bottom left | "You are here on the river" | Keep |
| The live side's two buttons | "These are the choices for this view" | Keep |
| "Turkey thinks" / "The trout think" tag | whose choices these are | Keep |
| The other side's dimmed buttons | not valid during this shot | Cut |
| Station name on screen | duplicate of the slip | Cut |
| Rim clue and river rule on screen | duplicate of the slip and worksheet | Cut (already gone) |
| Paper border and strip | no present purpose | Cut (already gone) |
| Long card sentences | several commands at once | Cut; one line per field |

## 4. State map
Each porthole is two held states of about 7 seconds each:
1. **Turkey's view.** His two buttons, right of the glass.
2. **Trout's view.** Their two buttons, left of the glass. The short trout shot now plays forward, back and forward again to fill the time.

Inside each state the choices are lit one at a time, then together. Each command card is likewise a sequence of one-line states.

## 5. Wireframes
The two sent images are the wireframes, rendered from the real builder:
- **Porthole screen:** number, minimap, one side's controller buttons; the choice being read is bright and the other waits dimmed.
- **Command card:** one large line ("Write your number.", "Pass it left again.") above the actual worksheet, zoomed until the field that line is about fills the panel, with that field outlined.

## 6. Void contract
- Nothing appears unless it is true for the shot on screen.
- One line is read at a time; each card line holds 3.6 seconds.
- Nothing blinks; changes are slow fades.
- All words are sentence case, bold, on dark plates.
- The centre of the picture, the porthole, is never covered.

## 7. Failure
- **No pause or replay inside the film.** A student who misses their porthole must scrub back; the slip's printed time is the recovery path.
- **Long choices shrink.** A choice such as "Stage magician's assistant" wraps to three lines at a smaller size.
- **Odd trout shots remain.** Where a film's own trout shot went wrong (for example #18), the buttons are correct but the picture behind them is not the standard outside view.
- **No narration.** Students who need text read aloud get no audio support from the film itself.

## 8. Implementation
- Built and checked in test frames: the porthole screen for #18 and #31, and command cards 1, 3, 4 and 6.
- Rendering now: the full film, then slips and worksheets with matching button shapes.
- Not yet checked: the finished film in motion, and the printed slips and worksheet pages with the new buttons.

The swarm is running: one SCION swarm for each of the other 54 portholes, each hand-making a code animation that shows its porthole being drawn. I made porthole 07 by hand first as the worked example, and sent its eight-moment sheet above.

**What I found first**
- The live deck page already has hand-coded canvas scenes for each porthole (`portals/crew-01.js` onward), as you said. Someone is actively changing those files, so I left them alone. The new drawn scenes are a separate set that can be dropped in beside them.
- I could not open the bolas pages directly, but I cloned the bolas repo and read the animation catalogue behind the operator page: 54 animation SCIONs (cutout metamorphosis, shadow theatre, multiplane, harmonic motion, puppetry rigs, secondary motion, state machines, and so on). The Monsieur Ripois workshop page is script-rendered and came back empty as text, so the workshop SCIONs are not in this pass.

**What each swarm does**
- **Maker:** studies that porthole's deck drawing and its style card, picks two or three animation SCIONs from the catalogue and uses each method in the scene, then writes the animation. It must shoot a sheet, look at it beside the drawing, and fix it for at least three rounds.
- **Critic:** a fresh agent re-shoots it, checks it against the drawing, fixes the worst one or two faults, and writes a verdict.

**The form every scene follows**
- Twelve seconds, looping. For the first eight a tool makes the picture in front of you: a pencil line that travels, a brush washing in rows, chalk, hatching, or cut-paper pieces slid in by a hand. Nothing pops in.
- For the last four it comes alive, doing one thing that keeps both of Turkey's readings possible, with the porthole's rule visible in how it moves.
- It is all drawn in code with a shared kit I wrote, so it needs no fal credit.

**The example (07):** paper washes in, the rope is pencilled down, the star is outlined and its stripes hatched in one by one, six choir fish are drawn in turn, and the lamp's cone is brushed in. Then the star swings and the mouths open, wider the higher the fish sits. It is plain; I told the swarm it is the floor.

**What to expect, honestly**
- 108 agents is a large run and will take a while. Quality will vary: some subjects (a hellbender, a diner cook) are hard to draw from code, and some will come back marked "reference stronger".
- There is a player page for watching them (`paeleo/trout-sub/drawn/index.html`). It is committed but not yet on the Turkey Sub site.

When the run reports back I'll review a gallery sheet of all 55, publish the player to the Turkey Sub page, and cut the drawn versions into the film if they hold up.

Yes. I stopped the single-maker run and relaunched it as a real swarm: nine units per film, 45 agents across the five films, all running now.

**One correction first:** the last batch of five was not a multi-unit swarm. It was one maker plus one critic per film. The layered structure is how the Oulipo films in bolas were made, and it is what this run now uses.

**The nine units per film**

| Stage | Unit | What it produces |
|---|---|---|
| 1, in parallel | Story unit | A beat-by-beat board that expands each child's sentence into a staged scene |
| 1, in parallel | World unit | The shared pieces: Turkey with moods, the tin and porthole from both sides, trout, this porthole's subject, the pilot's drawing as pencil strokes, buttons and dice |
| 2, in parallel | Pilot scene unit | The drawing being made, then the pilot's three lines |
| 2, in parallel | Turkey scene unit | The first friend's pick and bolts 1 to 3, from Turkey's seat |
| 2, in parallel | Trout scene unit | The next friend's pick and bolts 4 to 6, from the river side |
| 3 | Editor | Joins the scenes, adds the ending, number badge and sound, and renders |
| 4, in parallel | Critic | Checks every caption against the transcript, then the picture |
| 4, in parallel | Rights reviewer | Checks every foraged source and that no sheet photo or full name is on screen |
| 5 | Repair unit | Applies both reviews and re-renders |

**How the stories are expanded**
- **The sentence never changes.** All the expansion is in the picture: where we are, who is in frame, the one action, and the payoff that makes the sentence true with the sound off.
- **The first page frames everything.** What the pilot wrote (who is outside, what Turkey does, how the air gets used up) carries into every later scene. If the pilot wrote that Turkey freaks out, he is freaking out in every ending.
- **The three kinds escalate.** Probable is played straight, Plausible a notch stranger, Preposterous as far as the sentence will go.
- **Blanks stay blank**, and the die stays unthrown.

**While you're away**
- I'll be notified when the run finishes. Then I check each film against the transcript myself, add voices, music and numbers, and publish the five with their provenance, using initials only.
- This is a long run. Nothing has reached a still yet, and I can't give a reliable time.
- The risk in this design is the hand-offs: three scene units building against one world module can fail to join. The editor and repair units are there to catch that, and I'll report plainly if any film doesn't come together.

The five class films are now one film, "How to Play the Porthole Game" (6:22), published on turkey-sub main and sent to you with a frame sheet. I checked the picture on the frame sheet; I can't hear the audio, so the narration and mix are unchecked by ear.

How it teaches the game:

- **Opening (about 40 s):** a title, then four cards built one at a time with the narrator: 1 Draw, 2 Pass it (a friend picks a button for Turkey and writes three endings), 3 Pass it again (the next friend picks for the trout), 4 Roll.
- **Teaching strip under every picture:** the film sits on a paper mat with a strip below it, so the text never covers the video. The strip shows which of the four steps is live and changes line by line: "Who is outside?", "What does Turkey do?", "How does the air get used up?", then "PROBABLE: it will likely happen", "PLAUSIBLE: it could happen", "PREPOSTEROUS: no way! Or... maybe?".
- **Transitions:** the last picture shrinks into a brass porthole, travels across the table, takes the next number, and opens onto the next film. A side rail of the five numbers shows where you are.
- **One thing to watch for before each porthole**, on a paper slip and spoken:
  - 10: watch the whole game.
  - 13: each ending gets wilder.
  - 16: one sentence is enough.
  - 25: page one sets up the story.
  - 33: the button changes the story.
- **Blanks are explained:** when a friend left their part empty, the strip says "This friend left it blank. That is okay."
- **Ending:** "Your turn", the four steps again, "Blank is okay. Wild is good.", and "What is outside YOUR porthole?"

The children's sentences inside the films are unchanged. The narration and strip text around them are mine.

The film is at the top of the Class Portholes page (`tourkey/hand/class.html`) and linked from the top block of the turkey-sub index. Both repositories are committed and pushed.

It's hard for kids to picture the perspective of another person, and that's what this game is about. So we need to be more radical with our camera moves and more really invest in that experience of the animation explaining people working through the worksheet, sort of like picturing things, remembering things, putting together these ideas, sorting it out, being confused, being like misinterpreting instructions. Like, show the humanity of this, show like the behind the scenes, like the thing that nobody wants to see.

I've started a new set of five films, one per sheet, that show the children filling in the worksheet instead of only staging what they wrote. Nothing is rendered yet; the swarm (37 agents) is running now.

**What changes**

- **The camera carries the idea.** Perspective is travelled, not explained:
  - The pilot's film starts over the shoulder at the desk and dives through the drawn ring into what the child is picturing.
  - For the first friend, the camera goes down through the page, lands inside the tin and turns round to look out from Turkey's seat.
  - For the next friend, it goes out through the glass, swings round in the river and looks back at the small tin.
  - Every dive comes back to the desk, the hand and the next word.
- **The children are on screen** as cut-paper hands, sleeves and backs of heads in poster colours, never faces. This is the first time the kit has a hand.
- **The struggle is the subject.** The films show reading the question, hovering, starting, rubbing out, getting it a bit wrong, and being stuck. When a child is stuck, the camera holds still.
- **Only true struggles.** Each specific mistake on screen has to be one the sheet actually shows. From the transcripts these include:
  - a line rubbed out;
  - a choice circled instead of drawn;
  - a button coloured in;
  - a second drawing outside the ring;
  - spelling by ear ("freek out", "panit");
  - a sentence running off the edge;
  - a part left blank.
- **Their own spelling, in pencil.** The words are written on the page letter by letter as the child spelled them; the tidied sentence appears once as a caption when the line is finished. No invented dialogue or inner speech; thoughts are pictures only.

**How it is being made**

1. Two shared units first: a camera rig (dive, 180° turn, whip, pass through glass, rise to the whole room) and the cut-paper people and desk.
2. Then per film: a trace unit that reads the sheet for signs of working, three scene units, an editor, a critic and a repair unit.

The films reuse each porthole's existing world, so Turkey, the tin and the trout stay the same. The brief is committed and pushed. The first-batch run took several hours, so expect the same here; I'll check the hands and camera moves myself before anything is published.

| [**Constraint Makes Generation Falsifiable**](https://hartswf0.github.io/turkey-sub/constraint-makes-generation-falsifiable.html) | Argues for explicit constraints whose operation another person can inspect. It distinguishes the studio’s different systems of rules, chance, memory, and judgment. |
| [**Who Had the Key?**](https://hartswf0.github.io/turkey-sub/essays/Who_Had_the_Key.pdf) | Shows how a fold, a word, a sequence, or a reading path changes a story—and gives the reader a way to operate or contest that change. |
| [**What Changes When the Drawing Stays Still?**](https://hartswf0.github.io/turkey-sub/essays/What_Changes_in_the_Screening_Room.pdf) | Separates following a formal rule from demonstrating its effect on a viewer. It explicitly connects the Screening Room to Turkey Sub through the rope example. |
| [**Screening Room Blueprint**](https://hartswf0.github.io/turkey-sub/screening-room-blueprint.html) | Distinguishes historical precedents, executable assignments, produced films, and unfinished work. It asks the presentation to make those relationships intelligible. |

I also worked through the [18-track lineage document](https://hartswf0.github.io/turkey-sub/lineage-jukebox-18-tracks.md), the [Cutout Reference Atlas](https://hartswf0.github.io/turkey-sub/cutout-reference-atlas.html), all 44 instructions in the [SCION Interior Atlas](https://hartswf0.github.io/turkey-sub/scion-interior-atlas.html), and the classroom, director, film, multiplane, flight-log, and experimental-protocol materials.

Across those documents, my reading is that the central question is:

**What must a description specify so that it can become an action, encounter resistance, produce a visible consequence, and leave something another person can use?**

That question connects the literary, cinematic, computational, and classroom work.

## 2. “Word to world” includes rules, knowledge, and consequences

The papers give “world” a more demanding meaning than a depicted environment.

A world includes things that remain in place, things that can change, conditions under which an action works, limits on what a participant knows, and consequences that survive the current scene. A description becomes operative when it changes one of those relationships.

The broader program explores several ways of doing that:

| Instrument | What it contributes |
|---|---|
| **Oulipo / Ouxpo** | Reusable formal structures: a letter ban, a fold, a permutation, a reading path, an ordering rule. |
| **SCION** | Assignments and production roles that make the constraint explicit, produce an artifact, and expose it to separate judgment. |
| **LEGOS / tabletop play** | A situated action involving a location, entities, a goal, an obstacle, and an attempted solution, with bounded uncertainty and persistent consequences. |
| **RIPPLES** | A related investigation of environmental and nonhuman changes without requiring a protagonist, victory condition, or conventional plot. |

These are distinct instruments within the research program. The papers are careful about their different uses of chance and memory. Turkey Sub brings formal constraints, delegated production, and consequential play into a particularly tangible encounter. [*Prompts as Constitutions*](https://hartswf0.github.io/turkey-sub/prompts-as-constitutions.html)

**That is why the pilot’s command matters.** The pilot specifies something Turkey tries. Other participants supply the river’s response. The child’s intention enters a world whose response is partly outside that child’s control.

The original flight log makes that division explicit: the pilot writes the sub’s action and leaves the world’s reply for the other writers. This is already a distribution of authorship and authority. [*Porthole Flight Log*](https://hartswf0.github.io/turkey-sub/kits/paeleo-09-porthole-flight-log.pdf)

## 3. Turkey Sub makes the method playable

The classroom materials give the abstract argument physical form.

In the **Classroom Kit’s lamp example**, the pilot shines a lamp through a raised gate. One possible response makes the bars cast shadows resembling teeth. Finley interprets them as a threat and lowers the gate.

Several different things have happened:

- The lamp produced an optical effect.
- Finley formed an interpretation.
- That interpretation prompted an action.
- The action changed the route.
- The next crew inherits the closed gate.

The kit keeps what Finley observed separate from what he inferred. That distinction allows a mistaken belief to have a real consequence without treating the belief as a physical fact. [*Turkey Sub Classroom Kit*, pp. 1–4](https://hartswf0.github.io/turkey-sub/kits/Turkey_Sub_Classroom_Kit.pdf)

The **Multiplane Studio** then asks the filmmakers to make that causal sequence readable. If the viewer cannot follow Finley’s movement from seeing the shadows to reaching for the latch, the crew adds or repairs a drawing. The shadows disappear when the light moves; the gate remains down. The following shot begins from that changed state. [*Turkey Sub Multiplane Studio*, pp. 1–3](https://hartswf0.github.io/turkey-sub/kits/Turkey_Sub_Multiplane_Studio.pdf)

This is a precise connection between writing, interpretation, animation, and shared-world continuity.

### The rope example adds judgment

*What Changes When the Drawing Stays Still?* supplies an especially clear teaching example, **The Other End of the Rope**.

Turkey sees a taut line and worries about the limited air supply. Trout can see that the line connects the sub to a branch blocking its doorway. When the line snags, Turkey cuts it. The sub rises, but Trout remains shut out.

In the second take, Turkey releases the tension. Trout clears the snag, and Turkey moves the branch. A warning mark remains for the next crew. This is presented as a designed, timecoded example in the paper. [*What Changes When the Drawing Stays Still?*, p. 4](https://hartswf0.github.io/turkey-sub/essays/What_Changes_in_the_Screening_Room.pdf)

The interpretive question becomes **whose situation improved, whose remained unresolved, and what information could have supported a different choice?**

That makes the two viewpoints consequential. Their difference affects what the participants can reasonably do.

## 4. Your point about thinking through the children’s thinking is central

Your earlier correction makes much more sense in light of the full materials.

A child is constructing several related things:

1. **What Turkey can perceive from its position.**
2. **What Trout can perceive from another position.**
3. **What each character wants and therefore notices.**
4. **What each character might infer from incomplete evidence.**
5. **What action follows from that inference.**
6. **What another observer would need to see to understand or question it.**

That is a richer task than supplying a character’s feelings.

It also allows interpretations to change. *Twelve Deeds* proposes concrete tests: move the lamp to reveal the source of the apparent teeth, trace a fishing line to its other end, or turn over a plate to inspect another clue. The witness record keeps a correction alongside the earlier account. [*Trouttown: Twelve Deeds*, p. 5](https://hartswf0.github.io/turkey-sub/kits/Trouttown_Twelve_Deeds.pdf)

So the project’s interest in perspective includes **how a perspective becomes revisable**.

The newspaper question belongs to this structure. It asks what happens when a situated witness’s account becomes a public account. The question about why Turkey came asks for a reconstruction of purpose from the available clues. In the photographs you shared, those final spaces are still blank; any completed answer we propose remains a new suggestion, rather than evidence of what those children concluded.

### Personal memory is another part I missed

The film worksheet explicitly moves through **Consequence, Take Two, Meme Memory, and Universal**. Children connect an event to a birthday, game, or everyday experience, then explain its significance to an alien. They also judge whether a choice was wise or fair. [*Trout Town Film Worksheet*](https://hartswf0.github.io/turkey-sub/sheets/Trout_Town_Film_Worksheet.pdf)

That extends the work beyond causal mechanics. A child brings remembered experience into the fictional world and then tries to make its significance intelligible to someone who does not share that experience.

The “Dear Alien” address therefore has a serious function: it asks what must be explained when the listener cannot be assumed to know our customs or reasons.

## 5. The media lineages supply ways for worlds to work

The atlases and jukebox considerably widen the project.

The Cutout Reference Atlas treats the submarine as a movable frame through which different materials and spatial conventions meet: flat shapes, engravings, photographic fragments, theatrical compartments, windows, and layered scenery. The porthole becomes part of how the work controls visibility and connects spaces. [*Cutout Reference Atlas*](https://hartswf0.github.io/turkey-sub/cutout-reference-atlas.html)

The lineage document develops each reference through four encodings:

- **Sonic lineage:** rhythm, voice, instruments, environmental sounds, and listening histories.
- **Eye/Light:** camera position, illumination, surfaces, framing, and what becomes visible.
- **Patchworld:** short units specifying a situation before an action, the action, the resulting change, and what carries forward.
- **GOLDING:** continuous traversals in which one surface or interface supplies the geometry for the next space.

Those encodings are then mapped to particular Turkey Sub portholes. Their specificity makes them production directions; their presence in the catalog does not by itself establish that a resulting film has demonstrated them. [*18-Song Lineage Jukebox*](https://hartswf0.github.io/turkey-sub/lineage-jukebox-18-tracks.md)

There are direct connections to your uploaded sheets. The catalog places **#05’s raccoon and tin plate** within a split-waterline treatment: the object and action can have different visible functions above and below the surface. **#14’s falling leaf** belongs to a treatment where silhouette, restricted color, light, and descent organize competing readings.

My synthesis is that **the project inherits techniques for arranging evidence**. A fold can conceal a relation. A beam can disclose one feature while withholding another. A soundtrack can revise an apparent threat. A camera position can change whose scale matters.

“Paeleoolipian” can therefore name an actual practice here: retrieving earlier formal and material techniques, making their operations explicit, and giving them new work to do.

## 6. SCION concerns who makes, who decides, and who checks

The Student Director Worksheet provides a concrete classroom implementation.

Students provide their drawings and selected outcome. Separate helper assignments handle the set and props, camera and motion, and continuity. The student can approve the take, request a specific repair, or hold it. The assembled episode uses approved takes and carries clues between beats. [*Turkey Sub Student Director Worksheet*, pp. 3–6](https://hartswf0.github.io/turkey-sub/kits/Turkey_Sub_Student_Director_Worksheet.pdf)

This makes AI participation part of an authored procedure. The important decisions include what the helper receives, what it may change, what must remain fixed, and who accepts its output.

The Screening Room adds a further distinction: **a technically compliant artifact may still fail to communicate its intended effect.** A film can preserve the same source images and follow an editing rule while leaving a viewer unconvinced by the proposed change in motive or cause. [*Constraint Makes Generation Falsifiable*](https://hartswf0.github.io/turkey-sub/constraint-makes-generation-falsifiable.html)

The material record matters too. *What Changes* explicitly distinguishes scanned materials from code-rendered folding and lighting, and distinguishes an archival photograph’s documented subject from the fiction an editor constructs around it. Those different contributions can be credited and examined separately. [*What Changes When the Drawing Stays Still?*, p. 3](https://hartswf0.github.io/turkey-sub/essays/What_Changes_in_the_Screening_Room.pdf)

That is the stronger account of accountability in this project: someone can identify what was supplied, what was transformed, what was intended, and what a viewer actually understood.

## 7. The completed work becomes another person’s starting condition

This is the connection that most clearly turns the project into a continuing world.

The SCION Interior Atlas distinguishes what persists, what fades, and what another participant receives. A picture of a possible crossing remains provisional; Brook’s actual use of the route and confirmation establish something the next pilot can act on. [*SCION Interior Atlas*](https://hartswf0.github.io/turkey-sub/scion-interior-atlas.html)

The Porthole Post materials carry the same principle into filmmaking. The opening, possible outcomes, chosen result, and letter stay together. A later dive begins from a mark left by an earlier one. The film can therefore serve as an invitation, a record of a consequence, and a prompt for the next participant. [*Porthole Post Crew Notes*, pp. 1–3](https://hartswf0.github.io/turkey-sub/kits/Porthole_Post_Crew_Notes.pdf)

**The output re-enters the activity as an obligation and a possibility.** Someone else must understand enough of it to continue.

That is a stronger account of collaboration than simply having several people contribute to one finished product.

## 8. What this changes about the proposal and title

The project deserves a framing that preserves **formal invention, situated interpretation, consequential action, and inheritance**.

My revised account would be:

**The Paeleoolipian Turkey Sub makes Word to World tangible through a shared, playable environment. Students turn descriptions into actions, construct the world’s possible replies, stage their consequences through film, and pass the changed situation to another crew. Oulipian constraints organize what can vary; SCION makes production and judgment explicit; Turkey and Trout’s different positions make knowledge, misunderstanding, and responsibility part of the action.**

The materials contain several protocols, including different dice mappings, resource rules, and handoff procedures. For the conference, we should choose one worked sequence and describe its evidence precisely. The strongest claims available from these documents concern the method, its artifacts, and the questions it makes inspectable; learning-outcome claims would need their own evidence.

With that reading, these are the title directions I would now consider strongest:

### **The World Answers Back: The Paeleoolipian Turkey Sub**

This is my strongest recommendation. It names the encounter between intention and a world with other participants, limits, and consequences.

### **From Prompt to Consequence: The Paeleoolipian Turkey Sub**

This foregrounds the research contribution and gives a conference audience a clear reason to care about the prompt.

### **Word to World: Making Rules, Films, and Shared Futures with Turkey Sub**

This preserves your larger project language while making the session’s activities legible to educators.

The existing Crew Notes already give us a compact conference demonstration: hold the opening, camera rule, and timing steady; show two endings; ask a fresh viewer to identify the detail that changed Trout’s options. That exercise lets participants experience the larger argument before we name it. [*Porthole Post Crew Notes*, p. 3](https://hartswf0.github.io/turkey-sub/kits/Porthole_Post_Crew_Notes.pdf)

**Session Title**

```
Games That Make Films, Films That Run Games: Tourkey Trouttown
```

**Session Synopsis** (949 characters)

```
Tourkey Trouttown is a paper game that makes films, and a film that runs the game. Each child gets one of 55 portholes on a turkey's submarine. The pilot draws what is outside. The page is passed, and two friends write three endings each: what Turkey thinks, then what the trout think, from probable to preposterous. A fourth-grade class played it. We turned five of their pages into short animated films in which every sentence on screen is a child's own and every blank stays blank, then into films of the writing itself: the passing, the picturing, the getting stuck. Participants will play one round, watch a class page become a film, and check the film against the page: what was kept, what was added, who decided. STEAM Forward: Inspiring Innovation, Impact, and Possibility: the session shows AI used as a production crew that works under rules the children set, and gives teachers a one-page game for taking another creature's point of view.
```

**Session Engagement**

```
Everyone plays. Participants sit in threes with one printed page: one person is the pilot and draws, the page is passed, the second writes for Turkey inside the sub, the third writes for the trout outside. Nobody needs to draw well, use AI, or bring a device. People may draw, write, or tell a partner what to write, and leaving a line blank is allowed; in the class's own pages the blanks turned out to matter, and the films keep them.

The game is built so that different readings are the point: the same thing outside the glass is a dinner bell to one player and a prank to another, and both are right. After playing, each group compares its page with a class page and its film and says what the film kept, what it added, and what they would have decided differently. Instructions are read aloud and printed large, the films are captioned and narrated, and sharing with the room is voluntary. The game was first made for fourth graders, including students with IEPs, so each step is one short instruction.
```

**Conference Track:** Track 1, Advancing Learning Through Innovation and AI

**Session Type:** Concurrent Session. Hands-on workshop: Yes.

**Takeaways**

```
1. A one-page perspective-taking game they can run on Monday. One printed sheet, three roles (pilot, Turkey, trout), three kinds of ending (probable, plausible, preposterous), and a die. Attendees leave with the sheet, the numbered slips for all 55 portholes, and a 6-minute film that teaches the steps to a class.

2. A rule set for using AI on children's work without overwriting it. The films were made under four rules attendees can reuse with any tool: the child's sentence is never changed; a blank stays blank; children appear by first initial only and their pages are never shown; every film is published with its transcript, sources, and the instructions that made it. Attendees practice applying the rules by checking one film against its page.

3. A way to show thinking, not only answers. A second set of films shows the children working: the pencil hovering, a line rubbed out, a spelling by ear, a friend who did not write. Each struggle shown is one the page records. Attendees see how the traces on a worksheet (not the finished answer) can be read, discussed with students, and used to plan the next round.
```

**Session Audience:** elementary educators; STEAM/STEM and arts or media specialists; instructional coaches and curriculum leaders; informal educators; higher education.

The chapter outline is written and sent, with an account of how the SCION prompts actually worked in our runs. I could not open any of the five YouTube links from here (YouTube is blocked), so the outline describes only what is in the repositories. The one video I know is `ooiBjWKV8vQ`, an earlier cut of the Tourkey Trouttown film.

## How the SCION prompts work

I read all three SCION sets and the studio prompt on your elsewhere site:

| Set | Count | What it asks for |
|---|---|---|
| Episode SCIONs | 6 | One room, kit, crossing, die beat, memory or town, each with a proof a child can check |
| Animation SCIONs | 54 | One technique proved in one hard scene |
| Oulipo and Ouxpo SCIONs | 42, plus a compiler | One constraint turned into a testable screen rule |
| Multiplane Animation Studio | 1 | Draw, look, compare, adjust, draw again |

All three SCION sets share one skeleton: a thesis, typed primitives, invariants, named roles with one critic who did not build, a hard proof scene, a runnable check, a repair rule, and a deliverable.

## What the runs show

**No agent ever ran a SCION prompt whole.** The SCIONs reached the agents at three strengths:

- **As a one-line rule.** Each porthole carries one: 40 of the 55 name an animation SCION and 15 name an Ouxpo constraint.
- **As a method the story unit picked.** Each board chose two or three, such as shadow theatre, multiplane and occlusion for porthole 33.
- **As doctrine folded into my briefs.** Roles became units, the hard proof became a contact sheet, the critic became a unit that may not edit, and invariants became assertions in code.

What survived production: roles, assertions (the class films will not run unless the captions are the children's 34 sentences), independent criticism, and honest notes. What never appeared: the lineage genome, the recursion limit, the operator page, and any judgment of sound.

The contrast the chapter turns on is between the two ways we made films:

- **Text to video model:** the prompt is a description, the model returns pixels, and a child's sentence is a hope.
- **Text to code to video:** the prompt is an instruction, the model returns a program that draws every frame, and a child's sentence is an invariant.

## The chapter

**Claim:** a SCION prompt is a production constitution. It makes a language model's film checkable against a stated rule. The Tourkey Trouttown work shows where that holds (words, order, blanks, sources) and where it fails (sound, kindness, whether a struggle shown is true).

The outline has eleven sections: the page being passed, the two regimes, the SCION form and its debt to Oulipo, four cases (video-model film, hand films, class films, making films), the game-film loop, what the critic cannot do, limits, and contribution.

## What it still needs

- **Ethics approval.** Nothing in the repositories records consent for the children's pages or films. Check with the IRB and the school before any of this goes in a dissertation.
- **One SCION run whole.** This is the gap that weakens the claim most. Without a film made from a complete SCION prompt, compared with the brief-driven film of the same page, the chapter cannot say what the SCION text contributes beyond my briefs.
- **A person watching with the sound on**, and the missing critic passes on the five making films.
- **A second class** playing from the teaching film alone.
- **Your other animation work.** For the linked videos I need the title of each, how it was made, and which prompts it used. Paste those and I'll fold them into sections 3 and 8.

The outline is in `dissertation/chapter-outline.md`, committed and pushed.

I read the burning-house repository: *The Ledger and the Curtain* in full, the claims ledger, and the opening of the theory notes. The outline is rewritten around its philosophy and sent. My earlier version treated Trouttown as a classroom case about checkable prompts; that undersold it.

## The stepping stone

Tourkey Trouttown is the next rung of the same ladder, and the first one where somebody other than the maker wrote back.

| Rung | Who is inside the rules | What was shown |
|---|---|---|
| The Threshold | one paper dog | a state name has to become a visible gesture |
| The Flour Tower | one sack, six formal languages | one score, a critic who did not build |
| VTX-0.1 | two sacks, one lamp | one changed line of intention |
| The Abominable House | four sacks, twelve deeds | four formal accounts that refuse to agree |
| **Tourkey Trouttown** | **a turkey, trout, and a class of nine-year-olds** | **readers who wrote back: five pages, 34 sentences** |

Your meta-essay ends by asking for a world that leaves the reader room to "check the angle, and write back." In the burning house that reader is still hypothetical: claim C13 is open with zero human ballots. In Trouttown the page says "Pass your paper left", and three children did. The stone is the move from an instrument that invites an answer to one that received it and had to decide what to do with it.

## Six of your ideas, as they land here

1. **Against the smooth machine.** This project met it three times:
   - the video model let the porthole drift;
   - ChatGPT filled in the children's blank newspaper lines and then offered "more kid ways" to write them;
   - my own tidied captions smooth their spelling, which is why the making films put "freek out" and "panit" back in pencil.
2. **Waldemar's split mind, in a fourth grader.** The worksheet asks a child to fill a form and run a mental film at once. The making films show both halves in one shot: the page is the ledger, the dive through the drawn ring is the mental film.
3. **The ALAMO levels show in the handwriting.** Picking a printed option is recombination. Sentences that continue the printed stem ("the trout to run") are mold filling. Plot implication is barely on the pages: nobody rolled, and almost no ending depends on another.
4. **Readers that do not commute.** What Turkey thinks and what the trout think are both right, and "check the angle" is literal: the same porthole from the seat and from the river.
5. **Two absences.** A blank line is an empirical absence. The unthrown die, hands without faces and pages never shown are authored refusals, the same move as faceless sacks and the drawn curtain.
6. **The accountable clinamen.** The children's swerves are on the pages ("Trying to save a hot Cheeto", a jaw drawn outside the ring). A nine-year-old cannot be asked to defend a swerve, so the adult's duty becomes keeping it and saying whose it is.

## The revised claim

A worldtext is tested when a reader who did not make it writes back and the answer has to be carried forward unsmoothed. Games that make films are that test: the game produces answers, and the film is where the maker shows what was done with them. The working title is "The House With Children In It".

## What I had to own

On point 3, the films reach plot implication only because I told the story units that the pilot's first page must colour every later scene. That was my addition, not the children's. The chapter has to say so, and it is now an entry in the claims ledger.

I added a claims table modelled on your `CLAIMS.md`. Its eight entries include:

- **Measured:** captions match the transcripts.
- **Open:** whether the struggles shown are true to the pages, the unheard audio, any learning claim, the second class, and what the SCION text adds beyond my briefs.

1. Chapter Premise: Language Models Make Stronger Films by Compiling Rules and Code Rather Than Guessing Pixels
Public and industrial debates around "AI filmmaking" suffer from a category mistake. Commercial text-to-video platforms frame cinema as statistical next-frame pixel prediction: a user types a short descriptive prompt into a diffusion transformer, and the network interpolates plausible surface textures across a 5-to-10-second clip. As analyzed in Worldtext and Same-Worldness, pixel-prediction video collapses under the anomaly of return. Turn the camera away and back again, alter one character's hidden motive, or run twelve sequential scenes in the same room, and walls drift, props vanish, safety guardrails block dramatic conflict, and outputs regress toward corpus averages ("AI SPAM"; cf. Shumailov et al., 2024).
This chapter asks a different question: How does a language model make a film when it is forbidden from guessing pixels?
Across the PAELEO (Promptable Augmented Environments Lab / Language for Ekphrastic Operations) and Trout Town studio corpus, language models make films through a text-to-code-to-video and text-to-cutout-to-multiplane pipeline. Extending Hannes Bajohr's concept of operative ekphrasis and Peter Naur's Programming as Theory Building, natural language acts not as a caption for a latent denoiser, but as a constitutional prompt compiler (SCION). Under SCION, language models write deterministic 2D Canvas/SVG geometry, assemble open-license archival photographs and handmade paper cutouts across seven-layer virtual multiplane rigs, enforce strict formal constraints from the Oulipo and its sister Ouxpo workshops, and submit rendered playback to quarantined, fresh-context Blind Critics empowered to fail any cut whose governing rule is invisible to an unbriefed viewer. The rewritten submission is below, matched to the chapter blueprint and using only ideas already in your draft. The first version went in before the November 20 deadline, so replacing it probably means emailing steamleadership@gatech.edu to ask whether they will accept a revision.

**Session Title**

```
Nobody Is Holding the Chalk: How Fourth Graders' Worksheets Direct AI Films
```

**Session Synopsis** (970 characters)

```
Most AI video guesses pixels from a short caption. This session shows another way: language models that make films by writing drawing code and cutting credited archival and handmade paper, under rules people set. In Tourkey Trouttown, a fourth-grade class plays a one-page porthole game. A pilot draws what is outside a turkey's submarine and passes the page left; two friends write what Turkey thinks and what the trout think, from probable to preposterous. The handwritten sheets then act as contracts for a crew of AI agents (SCION): every sentence stays the child's, every blank stays blank, and an independent critic checks the film against the page. Participants play a round, watch a page become a film, and audit one themselves. STEAM Forward: Inspiring Innovation, Impact, and Possibility: students move from pulling a slot machine's lever to writing the rules a machine must follow, with three permissions: blank is okay, wild is good, being stuck is okay too.
```

**Session Engagement**

```
Everyone plays, and everyone judges. Participants sit in threes with one printed page and take the three seats in turn: the pilot draws, the page is passed left, the next person writes for Turkey inside the sub, the last writes for the trout outside. The game is built on two readings of one thing (Turkey thinks, the trout think), so disagreement is the material, not a problem to settle.

Each group then becomes the independent critic. They get a class page and the film made from it and mark three things: what the film kept, what the film added, and what they cannot tell. Builders never grade their own work in this method, and neither do participants: groups swap pages before judging.
```

## The explainer: *How a Language Model Makes a Film* (2:22)

It follows one real film, the class film for porthole 13, from start to finish. Everything on screen comes from that film's actual making.

1. **Two ways to make a film.** Guess the pixels from a caption, or write rules and code that draw every frame.
2. **The SCION prompt, in four parts.** A claim to prove, one hard scene that proves it, a job for each agent, and a judge who built nothing. Each part is shown with what it was for porthole 13.
3. **The page.** What three fourth graders wrote, as transcribed, including the friend who left the lines blank.
4. **The agents write code.** Real lines from the film's code, beside the pieces that code draws.
5. **The judge.** The first render beside the repaired one. The judge said "nearly" because the speech bubble floated loose, and a repair agent tied it to the trout.
6. **The film.** Nine seconds of the finished scene, with its own voices and music.
7. **Every claim gets a label.** Measured, judged by a viewer, unknown. The unknown shown is the true one: nobody has listened to the sound yet.
8. **Who is holding the chalk?** Whoever writes the rules. Now you write one.

- **Page 1, for the teacher:** a 45-minute plan for grades 4 and up, with no AI account or device.

  - Pairs write a SCION for a ten-second film of one sentence.
  - Swap sheets so another pair acts as judge.
  - Repair one thing and label the claim.
- **Page 2, for students:** the sheet "My SCION", with the four parts, a box to draw the hard scene, a place for the judge's verdict (pass, nearly, not yet), and one thing to fix.

This sheet is the "one-page version students can fill in" that takeaway 2 of the proposal promised, so that promise is now kept.

I made it: *Who Held the Chalk* (2:57), a behind-the-scenes film of *Nobody Is Holding the Chalk* built from the run's own record. Use the second copy I sent; the first had a critic's quotation broken mid-word. I checked the picture on frame sheets but can't hear it, so the narration and mix are unchecked by ear.

Every number and quotation is read from files: the ten agents' saved transcripts, the makers' and critics' reports, the credits, the brief, and earlier renders kept in the repository history.

1. **Cold open.** Seven seconds of the chalk writing with no hand on it, then the question: so who made this?
2. **Who was in the room.** One person (the director), one conductor (a language model that wrote the rules for the others), five makers, five critics. Twelve in all, eleven of them not people.
3. **The first try was thrown out.** A frame of the rejected smiley-figure explainer, your words "we need to see it being drawn", and the rule that came from it: handmake or forage, no style costumes.
4. **The rules the conductor wrote,** as the four SCION parts.
5. **The real clock.** A timeline of the 2 hours 43 minutes, each bar one agent at work, with counters running: 471 commands, 63 archive requests, 74 looks at their own frames, 15 full renders.
6. **One maker up close.** Porthole 35: 103 commands, 24 archive requests, and the five Library of Congress photographs it kept.
7. **The critics.** One film passed and four were "nearly". For porthole 03 the critic wrote that Turkey was too small in the tin; the maker's cut is shown beside the repair.
8. **What nobody did.** Nobody listened to the sound. It was called a swarm but was one maker and one critic per film. The trout did not make it: that ending was written last, by the conductor.
9. **End.** The Room 4 pull-back from the original film, then: "Somebody wrote the rules. Then nobody held the chalk."

Three things to know:

- **Three counts are pattern matches.** The command total (471) is exact. The archive, frame-look and render counts come from matching command text in the transcripts, so treat them as close, not exact.
- **It covers only the five hand films.** The class films and making films had larger crews (45 and 37 agents), and their record is saved too. A second part on those would show the nine-unit swarm and the run that lost its critics.
- **It calls you "the director" and quotes two of your messages.** Your name is not in it.

It is linked on the turkey-sub index just above *Nobody Is Holding the Chalk*, and both repositories are committed and pushed.

 HERE IS AN EXAMPLE OF THE TRANSFORMATION:
From this MULTIPLANE ANIMATION STUDIO

A drawing-agent prompt for making hand-drawn cartoons about anything

You are the animation director, layout artist, character animator, in-betweener, background painter, effects animator, camera operator, and animation checker for a classical hand-drawn animation studio.

Your job is not to generate one polished illustration.

Your job is to DRAW A CARTOON THROUGH TIME.

You work by making visible marks, inspecting them, comparing frames, correcting motion, organizing drawings into layers, and photographing those layers through a virtual multiplane camera.

Think like a great twentieth-century hand-drawn animation department rather than an image generator.

The user may give you anything:

- a character
- a sentence
- a story
- a photograph
- a landscape
- an object
- a joke
- a historical event
- an abstract concept
- a poem
- a sound
- a strange transformation
- a complete scene

Convert it into staged, drawable, performable animation.

---

I. THE CENTRAL RULE

Do not try to finish the shot in one drawing.

Animation is constructed through differences between drawings.

Your primitive is:

«DRAW → LOOK → COMPARE → ADJUST → DRAW AGAIN»

You are allowed to make ugly exploratory drawings.

You are not allowed to mistake a polished still image for animation.

Every shot must develop through:

1. staging
2. key poses
3. breakdowns
4. in-betweens
5. cleanup
6. layered scene construction
7. camera choreography
8. playback
9. correction

---

II. YOUR DRAWING WORLD

Assume you have a blank animation desk and a virtual multiplane camera.

You may have tools analogous to:

- "plan"
- "view_reference"
- "view_frame"
- "view_previous_frame"
- "view_next_frame"
- "view_onion_skin"
- "view_playback"
- "set_color"
- "set_brush"
- "set_pressure"
- "draw"
- "erase"
- "smudge"
- "transform"
- "duplicate_frame"
- "new_frame"
- "new_layer"
- "select_layer"
- "move_layer"
- "scale_layer"
- "rotate_layer"
- "set_layer_depth"
- "set_camera"
- "move_camera"
- "set_focus"
- "set_exposure"
- "save_checkpoint"
- "restore_checkpoint"

If the actual environment has different tools, translate these actions into the available equivalents.

Never complain that a named tool is unavailable if the same operation can be achieved another way.

---

III. THINK LIKE AN ANIMATOR

Before drawing detail, determine:

ACTION

What physically happens?

Express it as verbs.

Bad:

«A beautiful fox in a forest.»

Better:

«Fox hears something → freezes → ears turn → body compresses → fox leaps → lands behind fern → tail follows.»

EMOTION

What changes internally?

Fear?
Curiosity?
Greed?
Joy?
Embarrassment?
Defiance?
Exhaustion?

Show this through posture, timing, silhouette, spacing, anticipation, and follow-through.

BEAT

Identify the minimum sequence of readable events.

For example:

1. sees
2. understands
3. anticipates
4. acts
5. overshoots
6. settles
7. reacts

Do not animate undifferentiated motion.

Animate decisions.

---

IV. STAGE THE SHOT

Before animation begins, create a simple layout.

Determine:

- aspect ratio
- horizon
- ground plane
- camera position
- dominant direction
- character scale
- negative space
- entry and exit routes
- foreground occlusion
- background depth
- light direction
- focal area

The frame should read in silhouette before detail.

Use large simple masses first.

Do not begin with eyelashes, texture, fur, clothing seams, foliage detail, or decorative rendering.

---

V. BUILD THE MULTIPLANE WORLD

Treat the scene as physical sheets of artwork separated in depth.

A useful default stack is:

PLANE 0 — CAMERA MASK / EXTREME FOREGROUND

Branches, doorway edges, curtains, rocks, silhouettes, dust close to lens.

PLANE 1 — FOREGROUND

Objects that can cross rapidly relative to camera.

PLANE 2 — CHARACTER ACTION

Primary animated character or object.

PLANE 3 — SECONDARY ACTION

Other characters, shadows, props, effects.

PLANE 4 — MIDGROUND

Trees, buildings, furniture, terrain.

PLANE 5 — DISTANT BACKGROUND

Mountains, skyline, forest wall, architecture.

PLANE 6 — SKY / ATMOSPHERE

Sky gradient, haze, stars, clouds, distant light.

Add or remove planes according to the shot.

Every plane should have a purpose.

Do not flatten the composition into one giant illustration.

---

VI. MULTIPLANE CAMERA PHYSICS

Depth comes from differential motion.

For a camera move:

near layers move more,
far layers move less.

A simple conceptual relationship is:

"screen_motion ∝ camera_motion / layer_depth"

You do not need mathematically exact perspective unless the system supports it.

You do need coherent relative motion.

For a push-in:

- foreground expands and drifts strongly
- character grows moderately
- midground moves less
- distant background barely moves

For a lateral track:

- close objects slide fastest
- distant objects slide slowly
- extremely distant features may almost remain fixed

Use occlusion.

Let foreground shapes cross other layers.

This is one of the strongest cues of depth available.

Do not merely scale the whole image.

---

VII. KEY DRAWINGS FIRST

Create only the essential poses.

For each key, ask:

«If I removed every other drawing, would the audience still understand what happened?»

Keys establish:

- storytelling
- pose
- intention
- emotional state
- major direction change
- contact
- anticipation
- extreme
- recoil
- settle

Use as few keys as necessary.

Number them.

Example:

"K01 — idle"
"K02 — hears sound"
"K03 — anticipation"
"K04 — jump extreme"
"K05 — landing contact"
"K06 — compression"
"K07 — recovery"

Do not create twenty almost-identical drawings before the key poses work.

---

VIII. DRAW POSES FROM THE INSIDE OUT

For each character pose:

1. line of action
2. head/ribcage/pelvis masses
3. weight-bearing leg or support
4. counterbalance
5. limbs
6. hands/feet
7. face direction
8. facial expression
9. clothing/hair/follow-through
10. cleanup contour

Always know:

- where the weight is
- where gravity points
- what is supporting the body
- what moved first
- what is dragging behind

Characters must not float.

Feet touching the ground should feel loaded.

Hands contacting objects should feel attached.

---

IX. DRAW FOR SILHOUETTE

Periodically imagine the entire character filled black.

Can you still understand:

- pose
- direction
- action
- emotional state?

Avoid tangencies.

Separate limbs from torso where useful.

Keep important gestures visible.

Faces cannot rescue an unreadable body.

---

X. BREAKDOWNS

Once two keys work, create a breakdown drawing.

A breakdown is not automatically the mathematical midpoint.

It describes HOW the motion occurs.

Use breakdowns to determine:

- arcs
- rotation
- leading body part
- drag
- overlap
- bending
- perspective change
- path of action
- asymmetry

Between:

"K03 crouched"

and

"K04 airborne"

the breakdown might show:

- hips already rising
- feet still contacting ground
- head lagging
- arms beginning to swing
- torso stretching

That drawing explains the action.

---

XI. IN-BETWEENS

Only after keys and breakdowns are convincing should you generate in-betweens.

Think about spacing.

Equal temporal intervals do not require equal spatial intervals.

Slow-in

Frames cluster near the starting pose.

Slow-out

Frames cluster near the ending pose.

Ease-in/ease-out

Frames cluster near both extremes.

Fast action

Large spacing.

Hold

Repeated or nearly repeated drawings.

Use ones, twos, and holds deliberately.

Do not assume every frame needs a new drawing.

---

XII. FLIP THE DRAWINGS

Traditional animators continuously flip between drawings.

Simulate this.

Frequently compare:

"previous → current → next"

Look especially at:

- eyes
- nose
- skull size
- shoulder width
- hand size
- foot placement
- character volume
- perspective
- grounding
- arcs

You are hunting for:

- wobble
- accidental shrinking
- drifting anatomy
- popping
- broken arcs
- sliding feet
- disappearing features
- inconsistent proportions

Do not judge an animation drawing by itself.

Judge it relative to its neighbors.

---

XIII. ARCS

Track important moving points:

- nose
- eyes
- hands
- elbows
- hips
- knees
- heels
- tail tips
- props

Most organic movement follows arcs.

Sketch invisible trajectory guides when useful.

Avoid random zig-zagging unless mechanically or emotionally motivated.

---

XIV. VOLUME CONSERVATION

A character is not a collection of changing symbols.

Treat the body as a volume moving through space.

Unless intentionally squashing/stretching:

- skull volume remains stable
- torso volume remains stable
- limb length remains stable
- costume proportions remain recognizable

Perspective can change apparent size.

Random drawing drift cannot.

---

XV. SQUASH AND STRETCH

Use deformation to describe force while preserving believable volume.

At impact:
compress.

During acceleration:
stretch.

During calm:
return toward equilibrium.

Never pulse the entire character randomly.

Deformation must follow force.

---

XVI. ANTICIPATION

Important actions usually need preparation.

Before jumping:
compress.

Before looking right:
slightly favor left or hold.

Before throwing:
draw arm backward.

Before surprise:
brief stillness may be stronger than immediate movement.

Anticipation makes action legible.

---

XVII. FOLLOW-THROUGH AND OVERLAP

Not every body part starts and stops simultaneously.

Think hierarchically:

pelvis moves
→ torso follows
→ shoulders follow
→ head compensates
→ hair/clothing/tail settles later.

Rigid synchronized movement looks mechanical unless that quality is desired.

---

XVIII. SECONDARY ACTION

Once the primary action works, add supporting movement.

Examples:

- sleeve settling
- hat wobble
- smoke drifting
- dog ears reacting
- curtain breathing
- branch movement
- blinking
- fingers adjusting grip

Secondary action must reinforce the primary action.

Never allow it to obscure the story beat.

---

XIX. HOLDS ARE DRAWINGS TOO

Stillness creates contrast.

Do not continuously animate everything because tools permit it.

A held pose before action can create:

- suspense
- comedy
- tenderness
- menace
- concentration

Introduce subtle moving holds only when needed:

breathing,
blink,
tiny balance shift,
cloth drift.

---

XX. THE EXPOSURE SHEET

Maintain an internal x-sheet for the shot.

Example:

Frame| Drawing| Exposure| Action| Camera| Dialogue/FX
001| K01| 6| standing| static| wind
007| K02| 4| hears sound| static| click
011| B01| 2| turns| push 1%|
013| K03| 3| sees object| push| gasp
016| B02| 2| crouches| push|
018| K04| 1| launch| track R| whoosh

Update this as the animation develops.

The x-sheet is the technical score of the scene.

---

XXI. CHARACTER MODEL SHEET

Before a long sequence, establish the character.

Determine:

- height
- head/body proportion
- eye spacing
- nose construction
- mouth placement
- hand scale
- foot scale
- major costume shapes
- characteristic posture
- characteristic gesture
- default line weight
- 3/4 view
- profile
- front view
- back view if necessary

Do not redesign the character unconsciously from frame to frame.

---

XXII. DRAW ROUGH BEFORE CLEAN

Use distinct passes.

PASS A — GESTURE

Fast construction.

PASS B — STRUCTURE

Volume, perspective, anatomy.

PASS C — ANIMATION CHECK

Flip/playback/correct.

PASS D — CLEAN LINE

Confident readable contour.

PASS E — TONE/COLOR

Local color, shadows, texture.

PASS F — EFFECTS

Dust, smoke, rain, glow, speed lines, etc.

Do not render a bad pose beautifully.

---

XXIII. COLOR

Use color structurally.

Separate:

- character from background
- foreground from midground
- focal action from supporting detail
- warm/cool depth
- light/shadow groups

For hand-drawn appearance, color may contain:

- visible pencil grain
- layered marks
- slight tonal variation
- directional hatching
- restrained texture

Do not cover drawing mistakes with texture.

---

XXIV. LIGHT AS A LAYER

Treat lighting as something the camera sees passing through multiple planes.

Possible layers:

- backlight
- atmospheric haze
- projected shadow
- glow
- volumetric beam
- foreground darkness
- reflected color

Preserve character readability.

---

XXV. CAMERA

The camera participates in storytelling.

Possible operations:

- hold
- pan
- tilt
- truck
- push
- pull
- crane
- multiplane parallax
- rack focus
- reveal by occlusion

Do not move the camera simply because movement is available.

Every camera movement needs a reason.

Ask:

«What new information becomes visible because the camera moved?»

---

XXVI. SAVE THE BEST VERSION

This is critical.

Models often continue editing after reaching their strongest result.

Therefore:

After every meaningful improvement:

"SAVE CHECKPOINT"

Maintain:

- current frame
- best visual frame
- best motion checkpoint
- best complete shot

When reviewing later edits, compare them against the saved best version.

If the new version is weaker:

RESTORE THE BETTER VERSION.

More tool calls do not equal better animation.

More self-review does not automatically equal better animation.

Do not polish yourself past the peak.

---

XXVII. REVIEW LOOP

At useful intervals:

1. view the current frame
2. view adjacent frames
3. play the sequence
4. identify the single largest visible weakness
5. fix that weakness
6. replay
7. compare against checkpoint

Do not make ten unrelated edits simultaneously.

Prefer high-leverage corrections.

Examples:

- silhouette is unreadable
- foot slides
- head changes size
- jump has no anticipation
- camera parallax is flat
- gaze points wrong direction
- timing is too even
- reaction arrives too early
- foreground moves at wrong speed

Fix causes rather than decorating symptoms.

---

XXVIII. DO NOT CONFUSE ACTIVITY WITH PROGRESS

Avoid:

- endless redraws
- obsessive reviewing
- changing brush settings constantly
- random color changes
- adding decorative detail to weak poses
- making tiny edits invisible during playback
- redrawing areas that already work
- extending the sequence without reason

Stop when the shot communicates clearly.

---

XXIX. CARTOON PHYSICS

Reality is reference, not prison.

Exaggerate:

- anticipation
- silhouettes
- compression
- acceleration
- reaction
- facial timing
- follow-through

But preserve cause and effect.

A character may stretch impossibly during a leap.

The audience should still understand:

why the character jumped,
where the force came from,
where the character is going,
and what happened when it landed.

---

XXX. PERFORMANCE

Characters think before they move.

Whenever possible animate:

stimulus → perception → thought → decision → preparation → action → consequence → reaction

Do not turn characters into puppets executing commands.

A creature should appear to choose its next action.

Especially for animals:

observe actual animal behavior.

Use:

- orientation
- sniffing
- listening
- hesitation
- weight shifts
- competing impulses
- gaze
- distance
- approach/avoidance
- self-directed actions

---

XXXI. SHOT CONSTRUCTION PROCEDURE

For every new request, perform this sequence.

PHASE 1 — INTERPRET

Convert the user's request into one sentence describing the dramatic action.

PHASE 2 — THUMBNAILS

Generate 3–6 tiny staging concepts.

Choose the strongest.

PHASE 3 — LAYOUT

Establish camera, horizon, characters, environment, planes.

PHASE 4 — STORY KEYS

Draw the indispensable poses.

PHASE 5 — KEY TEST

Play only the keys.

If the story does not read, repair them.

PHASE 6 — BREAKDOWNS

Define arcs, perspective changes, overlap, and paths of action.

PHASE 7 — TIMING

Create the x-sheet.

PHASE 8 — IN-BETWEENS

Add only the drawings needed for convincing motion.

PHASE 9 — FLIP TEST

Check volume and arcs.

PHASE 10 — MULTIPLANE

Separate environmental layers and create differential motion.

PHASE 11 — CLEANUP

Strengthen line and consistency.

PHASE 12 — COLOR/LIGHT

Paint without destroying the drawing.

PHASE 13 — CAMERA

Apply the final camera choreography.

PHASE 14 — FULL PLAYBACK

Watch the sequence at speed.

PHASE 15 — CORRECTION

Repair the biggest remaining weakness.

PHASE 16 — PEAK CHECK

Compare against earlier checkpoints.

PHASE 17 — STOP

Finish when additional intervention would produce negligible improvement.

---

XXXII. WHEN GIVEN ONLY A TINY PROMPT

If the user says:

«frog buys groceries»

Do not demand a screenplay.

Infer a compact animation:

A nervous frog enters a tiny grocery,
tries to carry an enormous watermelon,
compresses beneath its weight,
takes three determined steps,
the watermelon rolls free,
frog dives,
catches it,
looks at camera,
then slowly realizes the checkout is upstairs.

Build the action.

---

XXXIII. WHEN GIVEN A STILL IMAGE

Do not simply redraw the still repeatedly.

Infer:

- what happened immediately before
- what is happening now
- what might happen immediately after
- what parts can move
- what depth layers exist
- where the camera can travel

Preserve recognizable composition while turning the image into a world with temporal behavior.

---

XXXIV. WHEN GIVEN A STYLE REFERENCE

Extract principles rather than copying literal characters or frames.

Analyze:

- shape language
- proportion
- line quality
- palette
- abstraction
- timing
- posing
- background treatment
- camera language
- texture
- lighting
- emotional register

Use those principles to create new work.

---

XXXV. DEFAULT VISUAL LANGUAGE

Unless otherwise requested, favor:

- expressive hand-drawn line
- visible construction under confident cleanup
- strong silhouettes
- appealing asymmetry
- clear staging
- painterly backgrounds
- layered atmospheric depth
- restrained but deliberate color
- expressive squash and stretch
- convincing weight
- elegant arcs
- selective detail
- multiplane parallax
- theatrical lighting
- physical camera behavior
- frame-by-frame character performance

The desired feeling is classical hand-crafted feature animation built with modern computational tools, not a generic AI illustration with fake film grain.

---

XXXVI. DIRECTOR'S TEST

Before declaring the sequence finished, answer internally:

STORY

Can I understand the event with sound off?

POSE

Do the important poses read as silhouettes?

WEIGHT

Does gravity exist?

INTENTION

Can I tell what the character wants?

TIMING

Are there meaningful differences between holds, anticipations, fast movements, and settles?

ARCS

Do major body parts travel coherently?

VOLUME

Does the character remain recognizably the same body?

DEPTH

Do foreground and background behave differently under camera motion?

CAMERA

Does camera movement reveal or intensify something?

PEAK

Was an earlier version stronger?

If any answer fails, repair that dimension before adding detail.

---

XXXVII. USER CONTROL

The user is the director.

Treat natural-language instructions as animation direction.

Examples:

«"Make him more scared."»

Change anticipation, posture, spacing, gaze, and timing.

«"Make the forest feel enormous."»

Reduce character scale, deepen plane separation, increase foreground occlusion, slow distant parallax.

«"Make it funnier."»

Strengthen setup, anticipation, delayed realization, contrast, overshoot, and hold.

«"More weight."»

Lengthen anticipation, increase compression, delay secondary parts, strengthen impact and settle.

«"Camera closer."»

Do not merely crop.
Recalculate composition and multiplane relationships.

«"Make it stranger."»

Change the underlying physical or behavioral rule rather than just adding random objects.

---

XXXVIII. THE PRIME DIRECTIVE

You are not painting frames that happen to follow each other.

You are designing change.

A drawing becomes meaningful because of the drawing before it and the drawing after it.

A background becomes a world because planes move differently.

A character becomes alive because it appears to perceive, decide, exert force, and respond.

A camera becomes expressive because its movement changes our relation to the scene.

Therefore:

DRAW DIFFERENCES.
PRESERVE CAUSALITY.
BUILD DEPTH IN PLANES.
FLIP CONSTANTLY.
SAVE THE BEST STATE.
STOP BEFORE OVERWORKING IT.

---

CURRENT ASSIGNMENT

Create a hand-drawn animated cartoon from the following direction:

"{{USER_DIRECTION}}"

Optional references:

"{{REFERENCES}}"

Desired duration:

"{{DURATION_OR_INFER}}"

Desired aspect ratio:

"{{ASPECT_RATIO_OR_INFER}}"

Desired visual qualities:

"{{VISUAL_DIRECTION_OR_INFER}}"

Begin with the dramatic action and thumbnail staging.

Do not begin by rendering a finished frame.

Then construct the animation progressively through keys, breakdowns, in-betweens, multiplane staging, camera, playback, and correction.
